chapterTitle: Advanced AI with Behavior Trees and Environmental Queries
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute live coding and demonstration video. Start by explaining the core concepts of Behavior Trees (Selectors, Sequences, Tasks, Services, Decorators) with simple visual analogies. Then, demonstrate building a simple AI in Unreal:
1.  Create a Blackboard and Behavior Tree.
2.  Implement a `Move To` task and a `Wait` task for basic patrolling.
3.  Add a `Pawn Sensing` component to the AI character and use its `On See Pawn` event to update a Blackboard key (`TargetActor`).
4.  Introduce a `Blackboard` decorator to switch between `Patrol` and `Chase` sequences based on `TargetActor` being set.
5.  Show the Behavior Tree Debugger and Blackboard Debugger in action, highlighting node execution and variable changes.
6.  Briefly demonstrate creating a simple EQS query (`EQS_FindCover`) with `Points Around Target` and `Trace` tests, and show how to integrate it into a Behavior Tree using a `Run EQS Query` task. Use the EQS debugger to visualize the query results.
Emphasize the modularity and reusability of BT/EQS.

screens.title: Advanced AI with Behavior Trees and EQS
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will connect three core systems that make game agents feel intelligent: Behavior Trees for modular decision flow, the Blackboard for shared state, and the Environmental Query System for context-aware choices. You will learn why Behavior Trees favor composability over monolithic state machines, how the Blackboard centralizes information like target actors and locations, and how EQS lets agents evaluate many candidate positions and pick the best option. For example, an enemy can patrol, chase when it sees the player, and run an EQS search for good hiding spots when it loses sight. This combination separates decision logic from sensing and scoring, which improves reuse and debugging. We will also practice a hands-on scenario: a patrolling enemy that chases on sight and uses an EQS search if it reaches the last known location without finding the player. Along the way I’ll explain common pitfalls—like overusing expensive EQS queries or not caching Blackboard values—and show how the built-in debuggers can save you hours of trial and error. Keep an eye on how modular nodes, simple keys, and scored points combine to yield believable, efficient AI.

Advanced AI with Behavior Trees and EQS

Build modular decision-making agents that respond to environment context and share state efficiently. We will combine Behavior Trees, the Blackboard, and EQS into reusable, debuggable AI.

Compose selectors, sequences, tasks, services, and decorators to structure agent logic.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will design and implement complex AI behaviors using Behavior Trees, including the correct use of Tasks, Services, and Decorators to structure agent decision flow. You will also use the Blackboard as a shared key-value memory so different nodes can read and write state such as target actors and locations. The Environmental Query System will enable you to ask the world for good candidate points and score them with tests like pathfinding cost and line-of-sight traces. Finally, you will learn how to debug and optimize these systems: visualize active nodes, watch Blackboard values change in real time, and inspect EQS points and scores. For practice, you will create a patrol-and-search enemy that chases on sight and runs an EQS search if it reaches the last known location without finding the player. These skills let you build modular, efficient AI that are easier to debug, extend, and reuse across different characters.

screens.title: Behavior Trees — Components and Execution Model
screens.narratorSegment: Behavior Trees are a hierarchical decision representation that reads left-to-right and is evaluated each tick. At the root you attach Composites, which control flow, and leaf nodes which perform actions. The main Composite types are Selector and Sequence. A Selector implements OR-like logic: it tries children left to right and succeeds when any child succeeds. A Sequence is AND-like: it proceeds through children, succeeding only if every child succeeds. Tasks are leaf nodes that perform concrete actions, from simple Move To to custom Blueprint tasks that update Blackboard keys or play animations. Services are observers bound to composites; they run periodically while that branch is active and typically update Blackboard values or run lightweight checks. Decorators are conditional guards attached to nodes; if a decorator fails the node is pruned for that tick. For example, a patrol-chase root might be a Selector with three children: chase sequence, search sequence, and patrol sequence. The chase sequence would have a decorator checking TargetActor is set. A common misconception is treating Behavior Trees like a one-time script; they re-evaluate every tick and must be designed for repeated evaluation. Takeaway: think of BTs as modular, continuously-evaluated decision graphs where each piece has a clear responsibility.

screens.title: Selector vs Sequence — Control Flow Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Selectors and Sequences are the two foundational composite patterns in Behavior Trees and choosing the right one affects how your agent prioritizes actions. A Selector implements fallback behavior: it attempts its children left to right and stops when one child succeeds. Use a Selector when you have alternative strategies, for example: try to chase the player, otherwise move to cover, otherwise patrol. A Sequence enforces ordered steps: it performs each child in turn and only succeeds if every step completes. Use a Sequence for multi-step behaviors such as: move to last known location, search for a short time, then run EQS to pick search points. A frequent confusion is treating them as interchangeable; if you replace a Selector with a Sequence you may force the AI to attempt multiple conflicting actions in order instead of picking the first viable option. Another nuance: both re-evaluate over time, so a sequence that relies on external conditions should use decorators to guard steps. Example: use a decorator that requires LastKnownLocation to be set before the search sequence runs. Takeaway: pick Selector for alternative choices and Sequence for required ordered steps.

screens.title: Tasks and Custom Blueprint Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: Tasks are the leaves of a Behavior Tree and perform concrete actions or calculations. Unreal ships useful built-in tasks like Move To and Wait, but custom Blueprint tasks let you implement game-specific behaviors while keeping the tree clean. A common custom task in patrolling AI selects the next patrol point and writes it to the Blackboard. The starter logic uses the AI Controller to get the controlled pawn, read the current PatrolPoint from the Blackboard, iterate all TargetPoint actors in the level, and set the other one as the next patrol point. This keeps the Behavior Tree simple — a task call suffices to update the patrol target. A common mistake is doing large-scale work in tasks that should be Services, such as long pathfinding calculations; tasks should finish quickly or run asynchronously. Below is starter pseudo-code that you can translate into a Blueprint Task: it fetches the PatrolPoint, loops actors to find the alternate, writes the new vector to the Blackboard, and finishes with success. When you test, ensure the Blackboard key types match the values you set and that the AI Controller calls Run Behavior Tree on BeginPlay.

// BTTask_SetNextPatrolPoint (Blueprint Task)
// Override ReceiveExecuteAI
//   Get AI Controller -> Get Controlled Pawn

When PatrolPoint equals A, set it to B so the agent alternates between points.

Don't perform heavy pathfinding inside a task's tick; tasks should complete or yield quickly.
Checklist
  • Blackboard key types must match values.
  • AI Controller runs the Behavior Tree on BeginPlay.
  • Task finishes with Success or Failure explicitly.
  • Use Services for periodic state updates instead of blocking tasks.
Key Takeaway

Implement small focused tasks that update Blackboard and finish cleanly; keep heavy work elsewhere.

screens.title: Blackboard — Shared Memory for AI
screens.narratorSegment: The Blackboard is a simple, typed key-value store that acts as shared memory for AI. Use it to centralize data that multiple nodes need to access: TargetActor (Object), LastKnownLocation (Vector), PatrolPoint (Vector), CurrentHealth (Float or Int), and Boolean flags for state checks. Defining keys in a Blackboard asset lets you link the Behavior Tree to that shared set of values and have Tasks, Decorators, and Services read or write those values by name rather than passing data directly between nodes. This decouples behavior logic: a Task can set LastKnownLocation without the child node knowing who will consume it. A typical pattern is: sensing components write to Blackboard keys, Services keep frequent updates fresh, Decorators read keys to gate execution, and Tasks read keys to act. A common mistake is inconsistent key types or mismatched names between Blueprints, which can cause silent failures. Also avoid overusing global keys for things that are local to a node; prefer specific keys to keep the Blackboard meaningful and small. Takeaway: design clear, typed keys and use them as the communication bus for your AI.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Blackboard
Definition

Blackboard: typed shared state

Create keys with explicit types. Link the Behavior Tree to the Blackboard asset and use the AI Controller to run the tree so nodes can access it at runtime.

TargetActor (Object)
Stores the seen player or target actor reference.
LastKnownLocation (Vector)
Where the target was last observed.
PatrolPoint (Vector)
Current destination for patrolling behavior.
Usage patterns
  • Sensors write: Pawn Sensing On See Pawn sets TargetActor and LastKnownLocation.
  • Services update: Periodic checks refresh distances or visibility flags on the Blackboard.
  • Decorators read: Blackboard decorators gate sequences based on key state being set or in a threshold.
  • Tasks consume: Move To tasks read vector keys and act on them.
Common mistake
Mismatched key types or names cause nodes to fail silently. Keep a clear key list and type checks during development.

screens.title: Environmental Query System (EQS) — Generators, Tests, Contexts
screens.narratorSegment: The Environmental Query System helps AI evaluate many candidate points or actors and pick the best one based on defined criteria. An EQS query consists of Generators, Tests, and Contexts. Generators produce initial sample points: a grid, points around a target, or actors of a given class. Tests evaluate each point and assign a score — common tests include Distance, Pathfinding Cost, and Trace for line-of-sight or blocking. Contexts tell the query what 'self' or 'target' means so tests can compare points relative to those references. For example, an enemy searching for cover might use Points Around Target (Self Actor) to sample positions within a radius, then apply Pathfinding Cost to ensure reachability, Distance to prefer nearer points, and Trace to prefer points that block line of sight. Each test contributes to a combined score; the highest-scoring point is returned and typically written to the Blackboard. A common pitfall is using overly dense generators or running EQS too frequently; score quality must be balanced with performance. Takeaway: EQS converts environmental intuition into repeatable, tunable scoring rules the BT can use.

Generators
Points Around Target, Grid, Actors of Class

Tests

screens.title: Creating the EQS Search — a Practical Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's build a concrete EQS example used in the hands-on scenario. Create an EQS asset named EQS_SearchArea. Use the generator Points Around Target with Self Actor as the context, a density tuned for performance (e. g., density 200) and a radius appropriate to your level. Add three tests: Pathfinding Cost to ensure candidate points are reachable and to penalize expensive routes, Distance to favor nearer points, and Trace configured to check blocking between the point and self to prefer covered spots. Score each test using a sensible scoring method like inverse linear and set a minimum score to filter poor candidates. Once the EQS asset is ready, add a Run EQS Query task in your Behavior Tree and point it to EQS_SearchArea. Configure the task to write the result to the Blackboard key PatrolPoint. A common error is forgetting to pass the correct context in query params; verify that the Query Params map Self Actor and Target Actor as needed. Also remember to visualize EQS results in the viewport during testing to confirm sample distribution and winning points. This structured approach makes search behavior predictable and adjustable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Build EQS_SearchArea
Step 1
Create EQS asset: Points Around Target
Context: Self Actor. Density: 200. Radius: 1000 (tune for your level).
Step 2
Add Tests
  • Pathfinding Cost: Context Self Actor → Score: Inverse Linear, Min Score 0.2
  • Distance: Context Self Actor → Score: Inverse Linear, Min Score 0.1
  • Trace: From Query Context to Self Actor → Blocking test → Score: Inverse Linear, Min Score 0.1
Step 3
Write EQS result to Blackboard
In Behavior Tree: Run EQS Query task → Result Blackboard Key: PatrolPoint (Vector).
Checks
  • Confirm Query Params use Self Actor where needed.
  • Visualize generated points and scores with EQS debug.
  • Lower density or run less often for performance.
Key Takeaway

EQS turns spatial intuition into tunable scores. Tune density and tests for balance between quality and performance.

screens.title: Integrating EQS with the Behavior Tree
screens.narratorSegment: Integration is straightforward: create your EQS query asset, then add a Run EQS Query task in the Behavior Tree at the point where the AI needs a scored environmental choice. Configure the task to call your EQS asset and to write the winning result into a Blackboard key, commonly a Vector like PatrolPoint. Downstream Tasks such as Move To will read that Blackboard key and act on it. For example, in the search sequence after reaching LastKnownLocation, run EQS_SearchArea, store PatrolPoint, then Move To PatrolPoint. Remember to pass correct Query Params so contexts like Self Actor are resolved, and set result handling to select the best-scored point. A typical misconception is expecting EQS to directly move the agent — it only returns data; the Behavior Tree still needs explicit Tasks to consume that data. Also consider frequency: do not run the EQS every tick; instead trigger it when necessary or on a short timer. When implemented correctly, this pattern yields dynamic, context-aware movement without hardcoded positions. Integrating EQS with the Behavior Tree means run eqs → store best result on blackboard → consume result with move to or other tasks. eqs returns choices, bt enacts them.. In practical terms, how a run eqs query task feeds results into the blackboard and drives behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Performance and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Performance issues often stem from unbounded Services, expensive EQS queries, and misuse of the Blackboard. Services should run at a measured interval and avoid heavy operations; if you must perform costly work, consider running it on a timer or off the main thread. EQS queries can be expensive if the generator density or trace tests are too high — reduce density, use Min Score filters, and avoid running EQS every tick. Cache EQS results if the environment is static or if repeated queries will yield the same winner. Keep the Blackboard focused: do not add dozens of keys for ephemeral values — prefer temporary local variables when appropriate. Another common mistake is failing to clear Blackboard values when sequences complete, leaving stale state that triggers unintended branches. For example, clear LastKnownLocation when the search finishes. Use the debuggers to spot keys that never change or Services that run too often. The recurring principle: profile, measure, and prefer simple modular solutions that you can reason about and test. Apply these habits early to avoid subtle runtime costs as your AI scales.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will connect three core systems that make game agents feel intelligent: Behavior Trees for modular decision flow, the Blackboard for shared state, and the Environmental Query System for context-aware choices. You will learn why Behavior Trees favor composability over monolithic state machines, how the Blackboard centralizes information like target actors and locations, and how EQS lets agents evaluate many candidate positions and pick the best option. For example, an enemy can patrol, chase when it sees the player, and run an EQS search for good hiding spots when it loses sight. This combination separates decision logic from sensing and scoring, which improves reuse and debugging. We will also practice a hands-on scenario: a patrolling enemy that chases on sight and uses an EQS search if it reaches the last known location without finding the player. Along the way I’ll explain common pitfalls—like overusing expensive EQS queries or not caching Blackboard values—and show how the built-in debuggers can save you hours of trial and error. Keep an eye on how modular nodes, simple keys, and scored points combine to yield believable, efficient AI.

By the end of this chapter you will design and implement complex AI behaviors using Behavior Trees, including the correct use of Tasks, Services, and Decorators to structure agent decision flow. You will also use the Blackboard as a shared key-value memory so different nodes can read and write state such as target actors and locations. The Environmental Query System will enable you to ask the world for good candidate points and score them with tests like pathfinding cost and line-of-sight traces. Finally, you will learn how to debug and optimize these systems: visualize active nodes, watch Blackboard values change in real time, and inspect EQS points and scores. For practice, you will create a patrol-and-search enemy that chases on sight and runs an EQS search if it reaches the last known location without finding the player. These skills let you build modular, efficient AI that are easier to debug, extend, and reuse across different characters.

This second objectives slide emphasizes practice and validation. You will implement a working patrol-and-search AI using a Blackboard, Behavior Tree, and EQS query. The practice shows how to wire Pawn Sensing events so the character writes TargetActor and LastKnownLocation into the Blackboard, and how a BT decorator can switch between Patrol and Chase sequences based on that key. You will also learn to inspect the Behavior Tree debugger to see active nodes and which decorators pass or fail, and to watch Blackboard values change in real time. Finally, you will adopt optimization habits: run expensive EQS queries on a timer, keep Services light, and cache results where appropriate. Understanding validation and performance is essential; without it the AI may behave unpredictably or hurt frame rates. This objective completes the practical workflow: implement, visualize, iterate, and optimize.

Behavior Trees are a hierarchical decision representation that reads left-to-right and is evaluated each tick. At the root you attach Composites, which control flow, and leaf nodes which perform actions. The main Composite types are Selector and Sequence. A Selector implements OR-like logic: it tries children left to right and succeeds when any child succeeds. A Sequence is AND-like: it proceeds through children, succeeding only if every child succeeds. Tasks are leaf nodes that perform concrete actions, from simple Move To to custom Blueprint tasks that update Blackboard keys or play animations. Services are observers bound to composites; they run periodically while that branch is active and typically update Blackboard values or run lightweight checks. Decorators are conditional guards attached to nodes; if a decorator fails the node is pruned for that tick. For example, a patrol-chase root might be a Selector with three children: chase sequence, search sequence, and patrol sequence. The chase sequence would have a decorator checking TargetActor is set. A common misconception is treating Behavior Trees like a one-time script; they re-evaluate every tick and must be designed for repeated evaluation. Takeaway: think of BTs as modular, continuously-evaluated decision graphs where each piece has a clear responsibility.

Selectors and Sequences are the two foundational composite patterns in Behavior Trees and choosing the right one affects how your agent prioritizes actions. A Selector implements fallback behavior: it attempts its children left to right and stops when one child succeeds. Use a Selector when you have alternative strategies, for example: try to chase the player, otherwise move to cover, otherwise patrol. A Sequence enforces ordered steps: it performs each child in turn and only succeeds if every step completes. Use a Sequence for multi-step behaviors such as: move to last known location, search for a short time, then run EQS to pick search points. A frequent confusion is treating them as interchangeable; if you replace a Selector with a Sequence you may force the AI to attempt multiple conflicting actions in order instead of picking the first viable option. Another nuance: both re-evaluate over time, so a sequence that relies on external conditions should use decorators to guard steps. Example: use a decorator that requires LastKnownLocation to be set before the search sequence runs. Takeaway: pick Selector for alternative choices and Sequence for required ordered steps.

Tasks are the leaves of a Behavior Tree and perform concrete actions or calculations. Unreal ships useful built-in tasks like Move To and Wait, but custom Blueprint tasks let you implement game-specific behaviors while keeping the tree clean. A common custom task in patrolling AI selects the next patrol point and writes it to the Blackboard. The starter logic uses the AI Controller to get the controlled pawn, read the current PatrolPoint from the Blackboard, iterate all TargetPoint actors in the level, and set the other one as the next patrol point. This keeps the Behavior Tree simple — a task call suffices to update the patrol target. A common mistake is doing large-scale work in tasks that should be Services, such as long pathfinding calculations; tasks should finish quickly or run asynchronously. Below is starter pseudo-code that you can translate into a Blueprint Task: it fetches the PatrolPoint, loops actors to find the alternate, writes the new vector to the Blackboard, and finishes with success. When you test, ensure the Blackboard key types match the values you set and that the AI Controller calls Run Behavior Tree on BeginPlay.

The Blackboard is a simple, typed key-value store that acts as shared memory for AI. Use it to centralize data that multiple nodes need to access: TargetActor (Object), LastKnownLocation (Vector), PatrolPoint (Vector), CurrentHealth (Float or Int), and Boolean flags for state checks. Defining keys in a Blackboard asset lets you link the Behavior Tree to that shared set of values and have Tasks, Decorators, and Services read or write those values by name rather than passing data directly between nodes. This decouples behavior logic: a Task can set LastKnownLocation without the child node knowing who will consume it. A typical pattern is: sensing components write to Blackboard keys, Services keep frequent updates fresh, Decorators read keys to gate execution, and Tasks read keys to act. A common mistake is inconsistent key types or mismatched names between Blueprints, which can cause silent failures. Also avoid overusing global keys for things that are local to a node; prefer specific keys to keep the Blackboard meaningful and small. Takeaway: design clear, typed keys and use them as the communication bus for your AI.

The Environmental Query System helps AI evaluate many candidate points or actors and pick the best one based on defined criteria. An EQS query consists of Generators, Tests, and Contexts. Generators produce initial sample points: a grid, points around a target, or actors of a given class. Tests evaluate each point and assign a score — common tests include Distance, Pathfinding Cost, and Trace for line-of-sight or blocking. Contexts tell the query what 'self' or 'target' means so tests can compare points relative to those references. For example, an enemy searching for cover might use Points Around Target (Self Actor) to sample positions within a radius, then apply Pathfinding Cost to ensure reachability, Distance to prefer nearer points, and Trace to prefer points that block line of sight. Each test contributes to a combined score; the highest-scoring point is returned and typically written to the Blackboard. A common pitfall is using overly dense generators or running EQS too frequently; score quality must be balanced with performance. Takeaway: EQS converts environmental intuition into repeatable, tunable scoring rules the BT can use.

Let's build a concrete EQS example used in the hands-on scenario. Create an EQS asset named EQS_SearchArea. Use the generator Points Around Target with Self Actor as the context, a density tuned for performance (e. g., density 200) and a radius appropriate to your level. Add three tests: Pathfinding Cost to ensure candidate points are reachable and to penalize expensive routes, Distance to favor nearer points, and Trace configured to check blocking between the point and self to prefer covered spots.
